chapter.name: Atomic Foundations of Matter
chapter.blurb: Builds on Chapter 8's atomic structure to ask what holds atoms together in compounds. Establishes the Law of Conservation of Mass and the Law of Constant Proportions through hands-on mass-balance activities, shows how Dalton's Atomic Theory explains both, then develops covalent bonding (sharing of electrons, naming covalent compounds) and ionic bonding (electron transfer, cations/anions, crystal lattice, naming ionic compounds), the criss-cross method for writing chemical formulae, the contrasting solubility/conductivity/melting-point properties of ionic versus covalent compounds, and finally molecular mass and formula unit mass calculations.

scope_in.item: Law of Conservation of Mass: Activities 9.1-9.3 (physical change, chemical change in open vs closed system, sodium sulfate + barium chloride), proposed by Antoine Lavoisier (1789); numerical verification (Examples 9.1, 9.2)
Law of Constant (Definite) Proportions / Proust's Law: fixed mass ratio of elements in a compound regardless of source, e.g. water H:O = 1:8 (Example 9.3)
Dalton's Atomic Theory: six postulates explaining the two laws above
Covalent bond: formation of molecules of elements (H2, Cl2, O2) and compounds (HCl, H2O) by sharing of electrons; single and double bonds
Naming covalent compounds: prefix system (mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, hexa-), vowel-dropping rule, hydrogen exception, common names (water, ammonia)
Ionic bond: formation of cations and anions by electron transfer (Na+, Cl-), electrostatic attraction, 3-D crystal lattice structure of NaCl
Naming ionic compounds: cation name first, then anion ending in -ide; monoatomic and polyatomic ions and their valencies (Table 9.1)
Writing chemical formulae of covalent compounds by the criss-cross-of-valencies method
Writing chemical formulae of ionic compounds by the criss-cross-of-charges method, brackets for polyatomic ions, simplification by a common factor
Properties of ionic vs covalent compounds: solubility in water vs kerosene/petrol, electrical conductivity in solid/dissolved/molten state, melting and boiling points (Activity 9.4)
Molecular mass of covalent compounds: sum of atomic masses of all atoms in the formula (Examples 9.4, 9.5)
Formula unit mass of ionic compounds: sum of atomic masses of all atoms in the simplest whole-number ratio formula (Examples 9.6, 9.7)

concepts.name: Law of Conservation of Mass
concepts.description: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction: the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products, provided the reaction is carried out in a closed system.
concepts.idea: In a chemical reaction carried out in a sealed (closed) system, the total mass of the products always equals the total mass of the reactants, because matter is only rearranged, not created or destroyed.
concepts.rule: Activity 9.1 shows that mass does not change during a physical change (dissolving salt in water). Activity 9.2 compares two set-ups for the reaction of vinegar with baking soda: in an open conical flask (set-up 1), the final reading is less than the initial reading because the carbon dioxide gas produced escapes into the air; in a set-up where a balloon traps the gas (set-up 2), the final reading exactly equals the initial reading, because no matter has left the system. Activity 9.3 repeats the test with sodium sulfate and barium chloride solutions, which react to form a barium sulfate precipitate and sodium chloride, again with no change in total mass. This is the Law of Conservation of Mass, proposed by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789: matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
concepts.example: Example 9.1: 4.0 g of calcium carbonate reacts with 2.92 g of hydrochloric acid; the products measured are 1.76 g carbon dioxide, 0.72 g water and 4.44 g calcium chloride. Total reactants = 6.92 g = total products (1.76+0.72+4.44), so the law is obeyed.

questions.q: 3.0 g of calcium carbonate reacts with 2.0 g of dilute hydrochloric acid. If 0.88 g of carbon dioxide and 0.36 g of water are formed along with calcium chloride, find the mass of calcium chloride formed, and verify the Law of Conservation of Mass.
questions.a: Total mass of reactants = 3.0 + 2.0 = 5.0 g. Mass of calcium chloride = 5.0 - 0.88 - 0.36 = 3.76 g. Total mass of products = 0.88 + 0.36 + 3.76 = 5.0 g, which equals the total mass of reactants, so the law is obeyed.
s: Mass of CaCl2 = 3.76 g

questions.q: A reaction is carried out in an open beaker and the total mass appears to decrease. A second student repeats the same reaction in a sealed flask and finds the mass unchanged. Explain this difference.
questions.a: In the open beaker, a gaseous product escapes into the air, so the measured mass drops; in the sealed flask, no matter can leave the system, so the escaped gas is included in the measured mass too, and it remains unchanged, showing that mass is truly conserved.
s: Open system loses gas, mass appears to drop
Sealed system keeps all products, mass is conserved

questions.q: Two students perform the same reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid - one in an open beaker and one in a stoppered flask with the gas trapped in a balloon. Analyse why only one of them can correctly claim to have experimentally verified the Law of Conservation of Mass, even though both used exactly the same masses of reactants.
questions.a: Only the student using the stoppered flask with the balloon can correctly verify the law, because that set-up is a closed system in which none of the carbon dioxide gas produced can escape before the final weighing; every gram of product, including the gas, is accounted for, so the initial and final masses will be found equal. The student using the open beaker will see a lower final mass, because carbon dioxide escapes into the air as soon as it forms and is never weighed, even though mass was not actually destroyed - it only appears reduced because the escaped gas is left out of the closed system's measurement.
s: Closed system correctly verifies the law (traps gas)
Open system loses gas before weighing
Explains mass is not destroyed, only appears reduced due to unweighed escaped gas

questions.q: A classmate claims that the Law of Conservation of Mass cannot be true because a burning candle clearly loses mass as it burns down. Do you agree with the claim? Justify your answer.
questions.a: No, I do not agree. The candle wax combines with oxygen from the air and burns to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the surrounding air; the total mass of the candle plus the oxygen consumed still equals the total mass of the wax lost plus the gases produced. The apparent loss of mass is because the system (just the candle) is open, not because mass is destroyed.
s: Disagrees, with reasoning about oxygen/gases escaping
Explains the open system still conserves mass overall

questions.q: Design a simple experiment, using a weighing balance, a conical flask and a balloon, to test whether mass is conserved when zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form zinc chloride and hydrogen gas. Describe your set-up and how you would interpret the result.
questions.a: Place zinc granules in a conical flask and dilute hydrochloric acid inside a balloon fixed tightly to the flask's mouth, so no gas can escape. Weigh the sealed set-up and record the initial reading. Tip the acid onto the zinc so the reaction proceeds inside the sealed system, trapping the hydrogen gas produced in the balloon. Weigh the flask and balloon again. If the final reading equals the initial reading, mass is conserved; if the same reaction were done in an open flask instead, gas would escape and the final reading would be lower even though mass is still conserved overall.
s: Describes a sealed set-up that traps the gas
Describes weighing before and after the reaction
Gives a correct interpretation, including why an open set-up would differ

concepts.name: Law of Constant Proportions and Dalton's Atomic Theory
concepts.description: In any compound, the constituent elements are always present in the same fixed proportion by mass, however and wherever the compound is formed; Dalton's Atomic Theory, built on this and the Law of Conservation of Mass, explains both by proposing that atoms are indivisible and combine in fixed whole-number ratios.
concepts.idea: A given compound always contains its elements in the same fixed mass ratio (Law of Constant/Definite Proportions, Proust's Law), and Dalton's Atomic Theory explains why: atoms are indivisible, cannot be created or destroyed in a reaction, and combine in simple whole-number ratios.
concepts.rule: Proust showed that water, however it is collected and purified, always contains hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1:8; sodium chloride always has sodium and chlorine in the ratio 23:35.5. John Dalton then proposed his atomic theory as six postulates: (1) all matter is made of tiny indivisible particles called atoms, (2) atoms cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction, (3) atoms of a given element are identical in mass and chemical properties, (4) atoms of different elements have different masses and properties, (5) atoms combine in the ratio of simple whole numbers to form compounds, and (6) the relative number and kinds of atoms in a given compound are constant. The two experimental laws motivated Dalton's theory, and the theory in turn explains why both laws hold.
concepts.example: Example 9.3: sodium chloride contains sodium and chlorine in the mass ratio 23:35.5. If 46 g of sodium reacts completely, the chlorine needed = (35.5/23) x 46 = 71 g.

questions.a: Yes, it is consistent. The ratio 4:2 simplifies to 2:1 when divided by the common factor 2, so both samples actually have the same simplest mass ratio of the two elements, which is exactly what the Law of Constant Proportions requires.

questions.q: A student finds that in one sample of an oxide of nitrogen, nitrogen and oxygen are present in the ratio 7:8 by mass, while in another sample believed to be the same compound, the ratio is 7:16. Analyse whether the Law of Constant Proportions has been violated, and suggest what might explain the difference.
questions.a: The Law of Constant Proportions has not necessarily been violated. A ratio of 7:16 is not a simplified or scaled version of 7:8, which suggests the two samples are actually different compounds (different oxides of nitrogen, since nitrogen forms several oxides), not the same compound measured with two different ratios. The law applies to one specific compound at a time: each distinct compound has its own fixed ratio, so two genuinely different oxides of nitrogen can each have their own fixed, but different, ratio without breaking the law.
s: Recognises 7:16 is not a scaled version of 7:8
Explains this suggests two different compounds, each with its own fixed ratio
Concludes the law is not violated because it applies per compound

questions.q: A classmate says Dalton's postulate 'atoms cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction' is the single most important idea for explaining the Law of Conservation of Mass. Do you agree? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Yes, I agree. If atoms could be created or destroyed during a reaction, the total number and mass of atoms present could change, so the total mass of products could differ from the total mass of reactants. Because Dalton's postulate rules this out - atoms only rearrange into new combinations - the total mass before and after a reaction must stay the same, which is exactly the Law of Conservation of Mass.
s: Agrees, with reasoning about atoms only rearranging
Connects this directly to why total mass stays equal

questions.q: Propose a simple experiment (different from the ones in this chapter) that a student could use to test whether a compound made from two elements always shows the Law of Constant Proportions, even when prepared in different amounts. Describe what you would measure and how you would judge the result.
questions.a: Prepare the same compound (for example, magnesium oxide, by burning magnesium ribbon) several times, using clearly different starting masses of magnesium each time - say 1 g, 2 g and 3 g - and burning each sample completely in a crucible. Weigh the magnesium oxide formed each time and calculate the mass of oxygen combined (final mass minus starting magnesium mass) for each trial. Then compute the ratio of magnesium to oxygen for each trial. If the Law of Constant Proportions holds, this ratio should come out the same, within experimental error, in every trial, regardless of the amount of magnesium used.
s: Describes repeating with clearly different starting masses of the same element
Describes the measurements needed (mass before/after, mass of oxygen combined)
States the correct judging criterion: same ratio across trials confirms the law

concepts.name: Covalent bonding and naming covalent compounds
concepts.description: Atoms that need to complete an octet (or duplet) can become stable by sharing electron pairs with another atom, forming a covalent bond; this is how molecules of elements (H2, Cl2, O2) and molecules of compounds (HCl, H2O) form, and covalent compounds are named using a prefix system.
concepts.idea: A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons to complete their octet; molecules of elements (like H2, Cl2, O2) and molecules of compounds (like HCl, H2O) both form this way, and are named systematically using number prefixes such as mono-, di-, tri-.
concepts.rule: A hydrogen atom (1 valence electron) shares one electron with another hydrogen atom to form H2 (single bond, H-H). A chlorine atom (7 valence electrons) shares one electron with another chlorine atom to form Cl2 (single bond). An oxygen atom (6 valence electrons) shares two electrons with another oxygen atom to form O2 (double bond, O=O). Atoms of different elements also share electrons: one hydrogen atom and one chlorine atom share one electron each to form HCl; two hydrogen atoms each share one electron with one oxygen atom to form H2O. Covalent compounds are named with a prefix system: mono- (1), di- (2), tri- (3), tetra- (4), penta- (5), hexa- (6); the first element keeps its name (mono- is usually dropped for it) and the second element's name ends in -ide; a prefix ending in 'o' or 'a' drops its last vowel before a vowel-starting element name (monoxide, pentoxide), but a prefix ending in 'i' keeps it (dioxide, trioxide); hydrogen as the first element never takes a prefix; a few compounds (water, ammonia) keep traditional common names instead of their systematic names.
concepts.example: CO2 is named carbon dioxide (not monocarbon dioxide); N2O5 is named dinitrogen pentoxide; H2S is named hydrogen sulfide, not dihydrogen sulfide, because hydrogen never takes a prefix.

questions.q: A student says that since hydrogen chloride (HCl) and water (H2O) both contain hydrogen and are both covalent compounds, they must be named using exactly the same naming rule. Analyse this claim using what you know about naming covalent compounds.
questions.a: The claim is not correct. Although both are covalent compounds containing hydrogen, HCl is named systematically as hydrogen chloride following the standard prefix rules (no prefix before hydrogen), while H2O is an exception that is not called by its systematic name (which would be hydrogen monoxide) but is instead known everywhere by its common name, water. So the general naming system does not apply in exactly the same way to every hydrogen-containing covalent compound.
s: Explains HCl follows the standard systematic rule
Explains H2O is a common-name exception, not literally called 'hydrogen monoxide'

questions.q: A student proposes that all molecules of elements (like H2, O2 and N2) must be held together by covalent bonds of the same strength, since they are all 'just two identical atoms sharing electrons.' Analyse this claim in light of the number of electron pairs shared in H2, O2 and N2.
questions.a: The claim is not correct. Although H2, O2 and N2 are each formed by two identical atoms sharing electrons, they do not share the same number of electron pairs: hydrogen atoms share just one pair (single bond, H-H), oxygen atoms share two pairs (double bond, O=O), and nitrogen atoms share three pairs (triple bond, N#N), because each element needs a different number of additional electrons to complete its octet (or duplet for hydrogen). A bond formed from more shared electron pairs is generally stronger, so these molecules are not held together with equal bond strength even though the general bonding principle - sharing electrons to complete a stable outer shell - is the same in each case.
s: Identifies the different numbers of shared pairs (1, 2, 3) for H2, O2, N2
Links this to each element's differing octet/duplet need
Concludes bond strength/type differs, so the claim is wrong

questions.q: Do you think the prefix-based naming system for covalent compounds (mono-, di-, tri-, etc.) is a good system for everyday use? Give one reason for and one limitation, using examples from this chapter.
questions.a: A reasoned answer either way is acceptable. For example: it is useful because it lets anyone work out the exact number of atoms of each element from the name alone, as in carbon dioxide (1 carbon, 2 oxygen) or sulfur hexafluoride (1 sulfur, 6 fluorine). Its limitation is that it is not always used - some very common compounds like water and ammonia are known by traditional common names instead of their systematic names (hydrogen monoxide, nitrogen trihydride), so a person unfamiliar with these exceptions could be confused.
s: Gives one reason it is useful, with an example
Gives one limitation, with an example (common-name exceptions)

questions.q: Two elements, X (which forms X2 molecules like oxygen) and Y (which needs one electron to complete its octet, like chlorine), combine to form a new covalent compound. Propose a plausible formula for this compound, name it using the systematic prefix rules, and explain your reasoning.
questions.a: Since X needs two more electrons to complete its octet (like oxygen) and Y needs only one electron (like chlorine), one atom of X would need to share with two atoms of Y, one electron pair with each, to become stable. A plausible formula is XY2. Using the naming rules, since X is the first element it takes no prefix, and Y (the second element) takes the prefix 'di-' with its name ending in -ide, giving the systematic name 'X diYide' - for example, if X were sulfur and Y were fluorine, the real compound would be SF2, named sulfur difluoride.
s: Reasons correctly about the electrons needed by X and Y
Proposes the formula XY2 with justification
Names it correctly using the prefix rules (di- on the second element)

concepts.name: Ionic bonding and naming ionic compounds
concepts.description: Atoms that can easily lose or gain a small number of electrons do so completely rather than sharing, forming positively charged cations and negatively charged anions that are held together by electrostatic attraction (an ionic bond), usually arranged in a repeating 3-D crystal lattice; ionic compounds are named with the cation first and the anion (often ending in -ide) second.
concepts.idea: An atom that can lose electrons transfers them completely to an atom that can gain them, forming a cation and an anion; the electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions is an ionic bond, and ionic compounds are named cation-first, anion-second.
concepts.rule: Sodium (1 valence electron) loses that electron to become the cation Na+ (11 protons, 10 electrons). Chlorine (7 valence electrons) gains one electron to become the anion Cl- (17 protons, 18 electrons). The electrostatic force of attraction between Na+ and Cl- is the ionic bond that holds sodium chloride together. Ionic compounds do not exist as separate molecules; they form repeating 3-D crystal lattices - in NaCl, each Na+ is surrounded by six Cl- ions and each Cl- by six Na+ ions. In naming, the cation's name is written first, followed by the anion's name, which usually ends in -ide for simple (monoatomic) ions; polyatomic ions (formed from two or more atoms, such as OH-, NO3-, CO3^2-, SO4^2-, NH4+) have their own valencies, listed in Table 9.1.
concepts.example: Magnesium (Mg2+) needs two Cl- ions to balance its charge, giving MgCl2. Sodium (Na+) and sulfide (S2-) combine as Na2S, since two Na+ ions are needed to balance one S2- ion's charge.

questions.q: Two students are asked to predict whether the sulfide ion (S2-) would form the compound Na2S or NaS with sodium. One student argues NaS is correct because 'one sodium and one sulfur is simpler.' Analyse this argument using what determines the ratio of ions in an ionic compound, and state the correct formula with reasoning.
questions.a: The student's argument is not correct, because the ratio of ions in an ionic compound is determined by the requirement that the total positive charge must exactly balance the total negative charge, not by which formula 'looks simpler.' Sodium forms Na+ (a 1+ ion) and sulfur forms S2- (a 2- ion, since sulfur has six valence electrons and gains two to complete its octet). To balance one 2- charge, two Na+ ions are needed, giving a total charge of 2+ that cancels the 2- of S2-. The correct formula is therefore Na2S, not NaS, which would leave a net 1- charge and would not be electrically neutral.
s: Identifies charge-balancing as the real rule, not 'simplicity'
Correctly states the charges of Na+ and S2- with reasoning
States the correct formula Na2S and explains why NaS is not neutral

questions.q: A classmate says that any two elements, one a metal and one a non-metal, will always form an ionic compound with a 1:1 ratio of ions. Evaluate this statement using at least one example from this chapter that contradicts it.
questions.a: The statement is not correct. While many metal-non-metal pairs do form 1:1 ionic compounds (such as NaCl, where Na+ and Cl- are both singly charged), this is not always the case. For example, magnesium chloride is MgCl2 (one Mg2+ ion needs two Cl- ions to balance its charge), and aluminium oxide is Al2O3 (two Al3+ ions and three O2- ions are needed to balance the charges). The actual ratio depends on the valencies (charges) of the ions involved, not simply on the fact that one element is a metal and the other a non-metal.
s: Disagrees, with reasoning about charge balance depending on valency
Gives a correct contradicting example (e.g. MgCl2 or Al2O3)

questions.q: Illustrate, step by step, how sodium sulfide (Na2S) is formed from sodium and sulfur atoms, including the electron transfer, the ions formed, and the final balanced formula.
questions.a: Sodium (atomic number 11) has one electron in its valence shell and loses it to attain a stable configuration, becoming a sodium cation, Na+. Sulfur (atomic number 16) has six electrons in its valence shell and needs two more to complete its octet, so it gains two electrons to become a sulfide anion, S2-. Since one sulfur atom needs two electrons but each sodium atom can only donate one, two sodium atoms are needed to supply the two electrons that one sulfur atom requires. The resulting ions combine in the ratio of two Na+ to one S2- so that the total positive charge (2+) balances the total negative charge (2-), giving the electrically neutral formula Na2S.
s: States sodium loses 1 electron each to form Na+
States sulfur gains 2 electrons to form S2-
Combines 2 Na+ with 1 S2- for the balanced formula Na2S

concepts.name: Writing chemical formulae by the criss-cross method
concepts.description: The formula of a covalent compound can be written by criss-crossing the valencies of the combining atoms as subscripts, and the formula of an ionic compound by criss-crossing the numerical charges of the ions, then simplifying to the smallest whole-number ratio and bracketing any polyatomic ion present more than once.
concepts.idea: Criss-crossing the valencies (for a covalent compound) or the numerical charges (for an ionic compound) of the two combining elements/ions gives their subscripts in the formula; a subscript of 1 is not written, the result is simplified by any common factor, and brackets are used around a polyatomic ion whenever more than one of it is present.
concepts.rule: For a covalent compound: (i) write the symbols of the elements, (ii) write their valencies, (iii) criss-cross the valencies to become each other's subscripts, and (iv) omit a subscript of 1. For an ionic compound: (i) write the cation's symbol first, then the anion's, (ii) write their charges below the symbols (not as superscripts in the working), (iii) criss-cross the charges as subscripts, and (iv) simplify the subscripts by dividing out any common factor. Charges are never shown in the final formula. Brackets are placed around a polyatomic ion only when its subscript is more than 1, e.g. Al(OH)3, not AlOH3; a single polyatomic ion needs no brackets, e.g. NaOH.
concepts.example: Criss-crossing Ca2+ and Cl- gives CaCl2. Criss-crossing Al3+ and O2- gives Al2O3 (no common factor, cannot simplify further). Criss-crossing Mg2+ and O2- gives Mg2O2, which simplifies to MgO.

questions.q: A student is given the ions Ca2+ and PO4^3- and is asked to find the formula of calcium phosphate. She criss-crosses the charges and writes Ca3(PO4)2. Analyse each step of her working to confirm whether it is correct, and explain why brackets are needed around PO4 but not around Ca.
questions.a: Her working is correct. Criss-crossing the numerical charges (2 for calcium, 3 for phosphate) means the charge of one ion becomes the subscript of the other: the phosphate ion's subscript becomes 2 (from calcium's charge) and calcium's subscript becomes 3 (from phosphate's charge), giving Ca3(PO4)2. Since 2 and 3 share no common factor, the formula cannot be simplified further. Brackets are placed around PO4 because it is a polyatomic ion and more than one of it (two) is present in the formula, so the subscript 2 must clearly apply to the whole PO4 group and not to just one atom within it; calcium is a single monoatomic ion, so it needs no brackets even with its own subscript of 3.
s: Confirms the criss-cross charges (2 and 3) are correctly applied
Confirms Ca3(PO4)2 cannot be simplified further
Explains why brackets apply to PO4 (polyatomic, count > 1) but not to Ca

questions.q: A classmate says the criss-cross method always works perfectly and never needs a follow-up check. Do you agree? Justify your answer using what you know about simplifying formulae.

Skipping this check can leave a formula that does not represent the true simplest ratio of the compound.

concepts.name: Properties of ionic and covalent compounds; molecular mass and formula unit mass
concepts.description: Ionic and covalent compounds differ systematically in solubility, electrical conductivity and melting/boiling points because of how they are held together; the molecular mass of a covalent compound and the formula unit mass of an ionic compound are both found by adding up the atomic masses of every atom shown in the compound's formula.
concepts.idea: Ionic compounds are generally water-soluble, conduct electricity only when dissolved or molten (never as a solid), and have high melting points; covalent compounds are generally soluble in kerosene/petrol rather than water, mostly do not conduct electricity, and have low melting points. Molecular mass (for covalent compounds) and formula unit mass (for ionic compounds) are both the sum of the atomic masses of every atom in the formula.
concepts.rule: Activity 9.4 tests camphor, sodium chloride, copper sulfate, sugar and naphthalene for solubility (in water, kerosene, petrol) and electrical conductivity (as a solid and dissolved in water). Ionic compounds like sodium chloride and copper sulfate dissolve in water but not in kerosene/petrol, and do not conduct electricity as solids (ions fixed in the lattice) but do conduct once dissolved or molten (ions free to move). Covalent compounds like camphor and naphthalene dissolve in kerosene/petrol but not water, and do not conduct electricity in any form; sugar is a covalent compound that dissolves in water but still does not conduct, because it does not form ions in solution. Ionic compounds generally have higher melting and boiling points than covalent compounds, due to the strong electrostatic attraction throughout the crystal lattice. Molecular mass = sum over each element of (its atomic mass x number of its atoms) in one molecule; formula unit mass uses the same calculation but for the simplest whole-number-ratio formula of an ionic compound, since ionic compounds do not form discrete molecules.
concepts.example: Molecular mass of H2O = (1x2)+(16x1) = 18 u. Molecular mass of CO2 = (12x1)+(16x2) = 44 u. Formula unit mass of Na2O = (23x2)+(16x1) = 62 u. Formula unit mass of Ca(NO3)2 = 40 + {(14+48)}x2 = 164 u.

questions.q: Metal M has two electrons in its valence shell and reacts with oxygen to form a compound that is slightly soluble in water. Predict (i) the formula of the compound, (ii) the type of bond it contains, and (iii) whether its aqueous solution would conduct electricity, giving reasons for each answer.
questions.a: (i) Metal M with two valence electrons would lose both to form M2+, and oxygen forms O2-; criss-crossing the charges 2 and 2 (which simplify to 1 and 1) gives the formula MO. (ii) Since M is a metal that loses electrons and oxygen is a non-metal that gains electrons, this is a transfer of electrons, so the compound contains an ionic bond. (iii) Because it is ionic, whatever small amount dissolves will release free-moving M2+ and O2- ions into the water, so its aqueous solution would conduct electricity, though only weakly given the low solubility.
s: Gives the correct formula MO with charge-balance reasoning
Identifies an ionic bond, with reasoning (metal loses/non-metal gains electrons)
Correctly predicts conductivity in solution, tied to ions being freed on dissolving

questions.q: A student tests two unknown white solids, P and Q. P dissolves in water and the solution conducts electricity; Q dissolves in kerosene but not in water, and does not conduct electricity in any form tested. Analyse which is more likely ionic and which is more likely covalent, with reasons.
questions.a: P is more likely an ionic compound, because it dissolves in water and its solution conducts electricity, both typical properties of ionic compounds whose ions become free to move in solution. Q is more likely a covalent compound, because it dissolves in kerosene (a typical solvent for covalent substances) rather than water, and it does not conduct electricity, consistent with covalent compounds generally not forming free-moving ions.

questions.q: A student measures the formula unit mass of sodium sulfate, Na2SO4 (atomic mass Na=23u, S=32u, O=16u), and gets 71u. Analyse her working to find the error, and calculate the correct formula unit mass.
questions.a: Her answer of 71u is incorrect. The correct calculation must include two sodium atoms, one sulfur atom and four oxygen atoms, as shown by the formula Na2SO4: (23x2) + (32x1) + (16x4) = 46 + 32 + 64 = 142 u. Her error was most likely counting only one sodium atom (23) instead of two (46), or otherwise missing part of the formula's atom count; either way, each subscript in the formula must be multiplied by its atomic mass and all the resulting values added together, which was not done fully.
s: Identifies her value 71u is wrong and explains the likely miscount
Sets up the correct calculation using all atoms in Na2SO4
States the correct final answer 142 u

questions.q: A classmate argues that molecular mass and formula unit mass are really 'the same idea with two different names' and that the distinction between them is unnecessary. Evaluate this view.
questions.a: The underlying arithmetic - adding up atomic masses according to the formula's subscripts - is indeed the same for both. However, the distinction is meaningful, not just a naming choice: molecular mass refers to a real, discrete molecule that exists as an independent covalent unit, whereas ionic compounds do not exist as separate molecules at all; they form continuous 3-D crystal lattices, so 'formula unit mass' correctly describes the mass of just the simplest repeating ratio of ions rather than claiming an ionic 'molecule' exists. So while the calculation method is shared, the terms correctly reflect a real structural difference between covalent and ionic compounds.
s: Acknowledges the calculation method is the same
Explains why the distinct terms are still meaningful, tied to molecules vs ionic lattices

questions.q: Design a simple classification test (using solubility and electrical conductivity, similar to Activity 9.4) that a student could use to decide whether an unknown white solid compound is more likely ionic or covalent, without knowing its chemical formula in advance. Describe the steps and how each possible result would be interpreted.
questions.a: Step 1: Try to dissolve a small sample of the solid separately in water and in kerosene (or petrol), and note which solvent(s) it dissolves in. Step 2: Using two electrodes connected to a low-voltage battery and a bulb, first test the electrical conductivity of the dry solid sample, then dissolve it in water (if soluble) and test the conductivity of that solution. Step 3: Interpret the results - if the solid is soluble mainly in water, does not conduct electricity as a solid, but its water solution does conduct electricity, it is most likely ionic; if the solid is soluble mainly in kerosene/petrol rather than water, and neither the solid nor any water solution conducts electricity, it is most likely covalent. A solid that dissolves in water but whose solution does not conduct (like sugar) would need to be treated as covalent despite being water-soluble, since conductivity, not solubility alone, is the more reliable indicator of ionic bonding.
s: Describes a solubility test step
Describes a conductivity test step (solid and dissolved)
Gives correct interpretation rules, including the sugar-like exception
